analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to count executive stock options as a real expense in their financial statements.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there with one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company pays its executives with stock options instead of cash, that pay is worth real money, but companies at the time did not have to show it as an expense. This bill ordered the Securities and Exchange Commission to require companies to subtract the fair value of executive stock options from reported profits. It would have made company earnings — the numbers investors and workers rely on — more honest, and would have made executive pay visible. The bill was referred to a subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and anyone who relies on corporate earnings reports, because company profits would reflect the true cost of executive pay instead of overstating them. Workers and the public also gain visibility into how much top executives are actually paid in stock, which at the time was often left off the books.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and anyone reading company earnings

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC to require companies to recognize the fair value of stock options granted to directors, officers, and senior executives as an expense in financial statements provided to security holders.

Requires the SEC to specify by rule how the fair value of the options is determined, and to issue final rules within 120 days unless the private accounting rulemaker (FASB) has already adopted equivalent standards.
Would have stopped companies from overstating profits: paying executives with options is a real cost, and leaving it off the books makes reported earnings look better than they are.

Congress was acting on the same problem the accounting rulemaker FASB had taken up that year — whether stock option pay must be expensed — with this bill as a legislative backstop if FASB did not finish.
The bill died without any hearing or vote, so companies continued to report earnings that did not count the value of executive stock options as a cost.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their senior executives, who would see reported profits shrink once option pay is counted as an expense, and whose generous option packages would become visible on the income statement.

drawbacks.text: Expensing options would lower reported earnings for companies that pay executives heavily in stock, which critics said would make many healthy companies look unprofitable and could discourage a pay-for-performance tool that links executive wealth to shareholder returns.
Valuing options requires estimates — the bill leaves the method to SEC rulemaking — and poorly designed rules could produce numbers that are noisy or easy to game.
The bill applies only to executive stock options, not options granted more broadly to employees, so the accounting treatment would differ across pay granted for the same kind of services.
The bill adds no penalties beyond existing securities law; its force depends entirely on the SEC writing and enforcing the required rules within a tight 120-day deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is honest books: investors and workers could see real profits and real executive pay instead of numbers that quietly omit a large cost. The cost is mainly on paper — companies would report lower earnings, not pay more cash — and the honest objection is that valuing options is an estimate, not a precise number. But the accounting rulemaking underway at the same time shows the underlying issue was real; the bill's method of pushing the SEC to act within 120 days was blunt but workable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it along to a finance subcommittee, where it sat until Congress adjourned with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Bryant of Texas introduced the bill on August 5, 1993, to require that stock option compensation paid to corporate executives be recorded as a compensation expense in corporate financial statements.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On August 13, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies and their senior executives, who kept reporting earnings that did not count executive stock option pay as an expense.

for.name: Rep. John W. Bryant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

for.name: One House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

for.name: Corporate executives and large public companies
for.what_they_did: Widely opposed requiring stock options to be expensed during the parallel FASB rulemaking of 1993-94, arguing it would depress reported earnings and stock prices.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were both Democrats, so the bill's support never grew beyond a single member of one party.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill would force option pay onto the income statement, shrinking reported profits and making executive compensation packages visible. Executives' interest in flattered earnings and understated pay ran directly against investors' need for honest statements.
Requiring the fair value of options as an expense would give investors and analysts more accurate earnings figures, the same goal the accounting standard-setter was pursuing in the same period.
The bill would give the SEC a new rulemaking mandate over executive compensation accounting, with a 120-day deadline to issue final rules unless private standard-setters act first.
